samples.text:
Traffic jam is a big problem in many cities around the world. Some people think the government should build more roads to solve this problem, while others believe it is better to spend the money on trains and public transport. This essay will discuss both views and give my opinion.

On the one hand, building more roads has some benefits. When there are more roads and wider highways, cars can move faster and people spend less time in traffic. This is important for businesses, because lorries need to deliver goods on time. Also, in countryside areas there is often no train or bus, so people have to use car and they need good roads.

On the other hand, many people believe public transport is a better investment. A train or bus can carry many people at the same time, so it reduce the number of cars on the road. For example, in cities which have a good metro system, many people leave their car at home and travel to work by train. Public transport also produce less pollution than private cars. In addition, some experts say that new roads only solve traffic for a short time, because more people start to drive when the roads are better.

In my opinion, governments should spend most of the money on public transport. It is good for environment and it helps more people, including those who cannot afford a car. However, roads in rural areas still need to be repaired and improve.

In conclusion, more roads can help traffic in short term, but public transport is a better long-term solution. Therefore, I believe the money should mainly go to railways and buses.
samples.why: Both views addressed and a clear opinion given · relevant but fairly general support · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · several agreement, article and verb-form errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Traffic congestion has become a serious issue in many growing cities, and governments must decide how best to address it. Some argue that building additional roads is the answer, while others believe investment in railways and public transport would be more effective. I am of the opinion that the second approach offers greater long-term benefits.

Supporters of road building make several reasonable points. New or wider roads can relieve bottlenecks and reduce journey times, at least in the short term. They are also essential for freight, as most goods are still delivered by lorry, and delays cost businesses a considerable amount of money. Furthermore, in rural areas where public transport is limited or non-existent, people depend on cars, and good roads are the only realistic way to connect these communities.

However, building roads rarely solves congestion permanently. When road capacity increases, driving becomes more attractive, and the extra space is often filled with new traffic within a few years. Public transport, by contrast, moves large numbers of people using much less space. A single train can replace hundreds of cars, reducing both congestion and air pollution. In cities which have invested in reliable metro or tram networks, commuters are often happy to leave their cars at home, which benefit the whole population.

In my view, the most effective strategy is to prioritise public transport in urban areas while maintaining the existing road network. Money should be directed towards frequent, affordable services that give people a genuine alternative to driving, and new roads should only be built where there are no practical alternatives.

In conclusion, although more roads can provide quick relief and remain important in rural regions, investing in railways and public transport is a more sustainable way of tackling traffic problems.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both views extended with relevant explanation · well-organised paragraphs with a clear focus · good collocations (relieve bottlenecks, road capacity) · mostly error-free with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Congested roads impose significant costs on economies and on the quality of urban life, and governments face a choice about how to respond. One view is that expanding the road network is the most direct solution; another is that the same funds would achieve more if spent on railways and other forms of public transport. While road investment has its place, I believe that public transport represents the better use of money in most circumstances.

The argument for building roads is intuitive. If traffic is heavy, providing more lanes should, in principle, allow vehicles to move more freely and reduce journey times. Roads are also indispensable for the movement of goods, emergency services and residents of rural areas, where population densities are too low to support frequent bus or rail services. For these communities, well-maintained roads are not a luxury but a lifeline.

Nevertheless, the benefits of road expansion in cities tend to be short-lived. Additional capacity makes driving more convenient, which encourages more people to drive and gradually recreates the original congestion, a phenomenon often described as induced demand. Public transport, by contrast, is inherently more space-efficient: a single rail line can carry far more passengers than a lane of private cars. Well-designed networks also bring wider advantages, including cleaner air, lower carbon emissions and greater mobility for those who cannot afford to drive or are unable to.

In my view, therefore, governments should concentrate urban transport spending on rail, trams and buses, while reserving road construction for areas where no viable alternative exists and for essential maintenance. The key is to make public transport sufficiently frequent, reliable and affordable that it becomes the natural choice rather than a last resort.

In conclusion, although building roads can offer temporary relief and remains vital in rural areas, investment in public transport provides a more lasting and equitable solution to traffic problems.
samples.why: Both views thoroughly developed with precise reasoning · clear, qualified position · logical sequencing and seamless cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (induced demand, space-efficient) · wide range of structures, error-free.
